nameStory: The celery leaftier moth gets its name from its larva's sneaky feeding habit - it literally ties celery leaves together with silk to create a protective shelter while munching away. The caterpillars are like tiny leaf architects, using their silk to "tie" or bind leaves into cozy hideouts. It's also called the greenhouse leaftier because it's a common pest in commercial greenhouses where celery and other crops are grown.
description: The celery leaftier moth is a small, brownish moth in the snout moth family, recognizable by its triangular resting posture and forward-projecting mouthparts that look like a tiny snout. These moths are about the size of your thumbnail when their wings are spread. The adults have mottled brown and tan wings that help them blend in perfectly with dried leaves and bark. While the moths themselves are quite plain, it's actually their leaf-tying caterpillars that gardeners notice first.

idTips.label: Snout-like mouthparts
idTips.description: Look for the distinctive forward-projecting mouthparts that stick out like a tiny elephant trunk when viewed from the side

idTips.label: Triangular resting pose
idTips.description: When at rest, the moth holds its wings in a steep triangular tent shape over its body, quite different from the flat wing position of many other moths

idTips.label: Mottled brown coloration
idTips.description: Wings have a rusty brown base color with darker brown and tan markings that feel papery to the touch, like dried autumn leaves

idTips.label: Small size
idTips.description: About thumbnail-sized with wings spread, much smaller than the chunky sphinx moths or large underwing moths you might see at porch lights

idTips.label: Leaf-tied larvae damage
idTips.description: Look for leaves (especially celery, spinach, or beets) that appear tied or webbed together - the caterpillars create silk-bound leaf shelters

habitat: You'll find celery leaftier moths in gardens, farms, and greenhouse areas throughout New England, especially where leafy vegetables are grown. They're particularly common around vegetable gardens with celery, spinach, chard, and beets, but also show up in flower gardens and disturbed areas with weedy plants. Look for them near outdoor lights at night during the growing season, or flutter up from vegetable patches when disturbed during the day.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring as temperatures warm. Look for the distinctive leaf-tying damage starting to appear on early planted vegetables and emerging wild plants.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period with multiple generations possible. Adults are most easily spotted at outdoor lights on warm evenings, while larval leaf-tying damage is most obvious on garden plants during the day.
seasonality.fall: Final generation adults may still be active in early fall. Look for fresh leaf-tying damage on late-season crops and the last adults visiting lights before frost.
seasonality.winter: Overwintering as pupae in plant debris or soil. No adult activity, but you might find old evidence of larval damage on dried plant material.

funFact: The caterpillars of this moth are such efficient leaf architects that they can tie together leaves from completely different plant families - you might find one shelter connecting a celery leaf to a nearby weed, creating a multi-species dining room with silk engineering!
confusionNotes: Many small brown moths look similar, but the celery leaftier's pronounced snout and steep triangular wing posture when resting are distinctive. Memory trick: "Snout out, wings up" - if you see both features together, you've likely found a snout moth in the Crambidae family.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a "pest" moth, celery leaftiers are actually native to the Americas and have been here much longer than our European vegetables - they've simply adapted to take advantage of our imported crops alongside their original wild plant hosts.
compareHints: Since this is the only Udea species commonly found in New England, compare it to other small snout moths in the Crambidae family. Celery leaftiers have more muted, rusty-brown coloring compared to the brighter patterns of grass moths, and their snout is more pronounced than most other crambid moths. The triangular resting posture is steeper and more tent-like than the flatter wing positions of similar-sized pyralid moths.
